concept.name: Outcome bias
concept.definition: The error of evaluating the quality of a decision by its realized outcome rather than by the information and reasoning available when the decision was made, demonstrated by Baron and Hershey (1988). Identical decisions are rated better when they happen to end well and worse when they end badly, even when outcomes are driven by chance.
concept.intuition: A reckless trade that made money gets praised; a disciplined trade that lost gets criticized - same process, different luck.
concept.mechanics: Evaluators weight the known result more heavily than ex-ante reasoning; experiments show the decisions of surgeons, coaches, and managers are judged worse after bad luck and better after good luck. In trading it rewards hidden risk-taking that happened to pay off and punishes sound process during normal drawdowns.
concept.failure_modes: It destroys learning: lucky gambles are reinforced and sound processes abandoned after ordinary variance. In performance evaluation it systematically encourages concealed tail risk, since only the realized branch of the distribution is judged.
concept.misconceptions: A good outcome does not validate a decision, and a bad outcome does not indict it - only ex-ante expected value and process quality do. Outcome bias is also distinct from hindsight bias, which concerns remembered predictability rather than evaluation of decisions.
concept.example: A desk praises a trader who doubled his account on an oversized punt and criticizes one who followed the risk plan into a losing streak; the punter blows up the following quarter.
